beats.say: When you move, a part of your brain called the cerebellum
beats.cap: WHEN YOU MOVE, | A PART OF | YOUR BRAIN CALLED | THE *CEREBELLUM*

beats.say: predicts exactly what you're about to feel.
beats.cap: *PREDICTS* EXACTLY | WHAT YOU'RE | ABOUT TO FEEL.

beats.say: Then it turns the feeling down before it arrives.
beats.cap: THEN IT TURNS | THE FEELING *DOWN* | BEFORE IT ARRIVES.

beats.cap: ADD A DELAY | OF UP TO | *A FIFTH OF A SECOND,*

beats.cap: AND THEIR OWN | TICKLE FELT | *MORE TICKLY.*

sources.fact: Sarah-Jayne Blakemore (UCL): the cerebellum can predict sensations when your own movement causes them; the prediction is used to cancel the response of other brain areas; a small delay between your movement and the tickle makes it feel tickly, and the longer the delay, the more tickly it feels

Blakemore, Wolpert and Frith 1998, Nature Neuroscience: the cerebellum is involved in predicting the sensory consequences of movements; with a robot interface, a progressive increase in tickly rating as the delay was increased between 0 and 200 ms
UCL: you can't tickle yourself because the cerebellum tamps down the brain's response ahead of time (Prof Sarah-Jayne Blakemore)

math.note: 200 ms = 0.2 s, a fifth of a second (Blakemore et al. delay range 0 to 200 ms)
a fifth of a second = 0.2 s

post.instagram_caption:
You can't tickle yourself. Your brain spoils the surprise 🪶

When you move, your cerebellum predicts exactly what you're about to feel and turns the feeling down before it arrives. In tickle robot experiments, adding a delay of up to a fifth of a second made people's own tickles feel more tickly.

Someone else's fingers can't be predicted, so you get the full tickle.

Sources: Scientific American (Sarah-Jayne Blakemore), Nature Neuroscience 1998, UCL.
